chunk_findings.detail: The two new pieces of documentation state opposite precedence for the diagnostics location. `DIAG_ENV`'s comment says the directory is "this variable, else `--diag-dir`, else `.ddflow/local/dryrun/`", i.e. the environment variable wins over the operator's explicit flag. The `Options.diag_dir` field comment says the field is what a failed run uses and "None: `DDFLOW_DRYRUN_DIAG_DIR`, else `<source>/.ddflow/local/dryrun`", i.e. when `--diag-dir` set the field, the flag wins and the env var is only consulted when the flag is absent. Concrete input: `DDFLOW_DRYRUN_DIAG_DIR=/var/log/ddflow` is exported and the operator runs with `--diag-dir /tmp/run7`; under the `DIAG_ENV` contract the transcript lands in `/var/log/ddflow` (possibly a shared, unwritable, or world-readable directory) even though an explicit directory was requested, while under the `Options` contract it lands in `/tmp/run7`. Whichever the code implements, the other statement is wrong about where a failed dry run's step table and stdout/stderr are written, and the two cannot both be authoritative for the environment-variable/flag interaction the intent calls out.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py:DIAG_ENV vs Options.diag_dir

chunk_findings.detail: `MAX_COMMANDS = 300` is documented as "The most commands a transcript keeps (the last ones)", but the failure report added to `Result.render` prints `diagnostics (every step's stdout and stderr): <path>`, and the module bullet added in the same change promises the file holds "every command's bounded stdout and stderr". For a long rehearsal — a full upgrade dry run can easily emit more than 300 commands — the earlier commands' output is silently dropped from the file, so the artifact the operator is pointed at is missing exactly the earliest steps, while the report claims it is complete. Demonstrable: run a rehearsal that logs 400 commands and force it to fail; the JSON contains only the last 300 commands' streams, but the rendered table asserts "every step's stdout and stderr" are in it. The cap and the message need to agree (either raise/remove the cap or say the transcript is truncated to the last `MAX_COMMANDS` commands).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py:MAX_COMMANDS vs Result.render

chunk_findings.detail: `live_moved` reports the union of `before.unstable` and `after.unstable`, i.e. shards that were already being written when the *pre-run* snapshot was read are surfaced as "the live shard {n} was still being written when read" and therefore make the run unavailable. That is a condition that existed before the rehearsal touched anything, so a live writer that was mid-append at snapshot time (and stops immediately after) is reported as a defect of the run. This is only masked by the whole-run retry; a writer that keeps churning makes every attempt fail. Arguably intended ("never as pass"), which is why this is only LOW.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py:live_moved / snapshot_live

chunk_findings.detail: The change adds `shard_bytes_checked` (which returns both the shard bytes and the list of shards that "never held still") but keeps the pre-existing `shard_bytes` as `return shard_bytes_checked(repo)[0]`, i.e. it deliberately throws the `unstable` list away while keeping the same public name and signature. Under the scenario this change targets — a live writer appending to/rewriting a shard while step 10 snapshots it — `read_stable` returns `(torn_data, False)`, `shard_bytes_checked` stores that torn `data` in `out` *before* checking `stable`, and `shard_bytes` hands the dict to the caller with no way to tell it is a torn read. Any call site that still snapshots the live shards through `shard_bytes` therefore cannot produce the promised named result `'live repo changed during rehearsal'`: instead the torn before-snapshot flows into `prefixes_kept(before, after)`, which can report a phantom prefix loss (the same "unexplained dry-run failure under concurrent live writers," bug B-dryrun-flake), or, if the same torn bytes happen to land in both snapshots, a pass. The intent explicitly requires the rewrite to be reported as unavailable and "never as pass"; a lossy public wrapper that discards the only instability signal preserves exactly that hole. Either `shard_bytes` should be removed/guarded so all live-shard reads go through `shard_bytes_checked`, or it must not silently return bytes for shards whose `stable` flag is false.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py: `shard_bytes`

chunk_findings.detail: `add`'s second positional is the step's *display name* and the third is the *status* — see the two neighbouring calls in the same method, which pass the fixed name `"live project untouched"` with `False` (leaks) and `True` (clean). In the `moved` branch the author instead passes the outcome constant `LIVE_CHANGED` in the name slot and `None` in the status slot. Given input where a concurrent live writer rewrites a live shard (so `live_leaks(...)` is empty and `live_moved(...)` is non-empty), step 10 is recorded as a step *named* "live repo changed during rehearsal" with a null status. The named unavailable result the change promises ("reports a rewrite of a live shard as the named unavailable result … never as pass") therefore never lands in the status field: any consumer that keys on the status — the report renderer mapping a falsy status to FAIL, or the whole-run-retry check looking for the `LIVE_CHANGED` status — sees `None`/FAIL rather than the unavailable result, so a shard rewritten by another agent is reported as an ordinary failure. That is exactly the "upgrade-dry-run fails unexplained under concurrent live writers" symptom this change is meant to remove. The intended call is `self.add(10, name, LIVE_CHANGED, detail)` (name stays `"live project untouched"`, status carries the named unavailable result).
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py `judge_live` (`self.add(10, LIVE_CHANGED, None, ...)`)

chunk_findings.detail: For a retried rehearsal, diagnostics mix runs: `write_diagnostics` tags the file and the `"run"` field with `runs[-1].run_id` and serializes only the final report's `table`/`checks`, but flattens `commands` from every run in `runs` with no run attribution. Given the motivating case — run1 sets `live_changed` (and can carry a `FAIL`), the retry run2 also detects a change — the emitted file is stamped with run2's id yet contains run1's commands, and run1's step table/checks are dropped, so the failure evidence the feature exists to capture is missing/misattributed.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py:write_diagnostics (called from run_all)

chunk_findings.detail: The two documentation comments in this part still state opposite precedence for the diagnostics directory. `DIAG_ENV` is commented "Where a failed run's step table and command transcript go: this variable, else `--diag-dir`, else `.ddflow/local/dryrun/` in the project", i.e. the environment variable overrides the operator's explicit `--diag-dir`. But the new `Options.diag_dir` field is commented "Where a failed run writes its transcript; None: `DDFLOW_DRYRUN_DIAG_DIR`, else `<source>/.ddflow/local/dryrun`", i.e. an explicitly set `--diag-dir` is used as-is and the env var is consulted only when the field is `None` (flag wins). Given `--diag-dir /tmp/a` and `DDFLOW_DRYRUN_DIAG_DIR=/tmp/b`, the two comments predict different output locations, so which one is authoritative cannot be determined from the change. The diff adds both comments in the same change and does not reconcile them.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py: DIAG_ENV vs Options.diag_dir

chunk_findings.detail: `MAX_COMMANDS = 300` is documented as "The most commands a transcript keeps (the last ones)", so a transcript longer than 300 commands silently drops the earliest entries. The same change, however, adds a module bullet promising the file holds "every command's bounded stdout and stderr", and `Result.render` (part 1) prints `f"diagnostics (every step's stdout and stderr): {self.diagnostics}"`. For a full upgrade dry run that emits more than 300 commands — plausible for the long rehearsals this diagnostic artifact exists to debug — the file referenced by that row does not contain the earlier steps' output, while both the row and the module docstring assert that every command's stdout/stderr is present. The operator reading the failure report to explain an otherwise unexplained flake is pointed at an incomplete artifact under a label claiming completeness.

chunk_findings.detail: `live_moved` reports the *union* of the shards that never held still before the run and after it. Given a live writer that was mid-append when the pre-run `snapshot_live` read shard `n` and then stops, `before.unstable == [n]` while `after.unstable == []`; the run reports `the live shard n was still being written when read` and is marked unavailable even though nothing rewrote the shard. Because `snapshot_live` is also used for the post-run read, a writer that just happens to append while the after-snapshot is taken (an explicitly allowed "the log may GROW") produces the same result on both the run and its one whole-run retry, i.e. a benign concurrent writer still yields an unexplained/unattributable failure — the class of bug this change targets. The change here is unchanged in the diff, so the previous finding is not answered.

chunk_findings.detail: For backups the leak test is `set(after.backups) - set(before.backups)` filtered by `mine.started <= b.partition("-")[0] <= mine.ended and backup_versions(b) in mine.versions`. Backups carry no run id, so unlike the tag path they are not attributed to the rehearsal at all — the stated intent ("attributes snapshot tags/backups to the rehearsal by run id") is not met. Input: while a rehearsal of `1-to-2` is running, another agent or an operator creates a backup `<stamp>-1-to-2` for the same live project; the stamp falls inside the rehearsal's window, the versions match, so `live_leaks` reports `a backup of the rehearsal appeared in the live project`, the run is marked unavailable, and after the whole-run retry (overlapping windows) it is still reported — a false hard failure produced by exactly the concurrent-actor situation this change is meant to tolerate.

chunk_findings.detail: New: a shard that a concurrent writer removes while the live read is in progress is silently dropped, not reported. `read_stable` wraps the whole `stat`/`read_bytes`/`stat` block in `except FileNotFoundError: return None, True` — so a `FileNotFoundError` raised by `path.read_bytes()` or the trailing `path.stat()` (i.e. the shard existed at the first `stat` but was unlinked/replaced during the read) is classified as "gone, stable", and `shard_bytes_checked` then `continue`s (`# removed since the listing: another agent's doing, not a failure`), omitting the shard from both `out` and `unstable`. Input: a live writer that truncates-and-recreates a shard (temp file + rename, or unlink + recreate) between `first = path.stat()` and `path.read_bytes()`; the rehearsal's leaked writes into that shard are erased, the shard never appears in `unstable`, and step 10 never produces the named unavailable result "live repo changed during rehearsal" — the run can pass while the live repo demonstrably changed under it. If the shard is recreated after the loop, it is never re-listed either, since `root.glob("*.jsonl")` is evaluated once.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py:read_stable / shard_bytes_checked

chunk_findings.detail: `footprint()` claims to return "what the rehearsal's own backups and snapshot tags (in the clones) are called", but it derives that identity purely as a set of *version* strings: it strips `SNAPSHOT_PREFIX` from each tag and runs `backup_versions(...)` over it, then hands `frozenset(versions)` to `Footprint`. Nothing in that set carries the run id the intent says attribution is keyed on, so `live_leaks(before, after, mine)` can only decide "this live tag/backup is the rehearsal's" by version. The motivating scenario makes this wrong: two concurrent dry runs of the same source produce the same tag/backup version (identical `SNAPSHOT_PREFIX<version>` names, since the name has no run id in it), so a tag or backup created in the live project by the *other* run lands in `mine`, is reported as this rehearsal's leak, and step 10 fails — the same unexplained failure under concurrent writers that this change exists to remove. The same over-attribution happens without any second run: `git clone --local` copies the live repo's refs/tags into `self.pristine`, so every `SNAPSHOT_PREFIX*` tag that already existed in the live repo at clone time is in the clone and therefore in `mine`, although the rehearsal never created it; a corresponding live tag is then attributable to this run. Conversely `judge_live`'s `others = set(after.tags) - set(before.tags)` (line ~806) uses a bare set difference with no run-id check either, so a genuine rehearsal leak whose version is not in `mine` is silently relabelled "made by others meanwhile and ignored" and the run passes. Either remove the tag scan (clone tags are the live repo's, not the rehearsal's) or key the footprint on the run id that the intent promises.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py `footprint` (called from `judge_live`)

chunk_findings.detail: Step 10 still hands the *pre-run* snapshot to `live_moved` and then treats any non-empty result as "the project moved under the run". `before` is the live read taken before the rehearsal started, so a shard that a live writer happened to be mid-append on at that instant (writer stops immediately afterwards, never touches the repo again while the dry run proceeds) is folded into `moved`, and step 10 is recorded as `LIVE_CHANGED` with the detail "...the project moved under the run, so it cannot be said to be untouched" — a condition that existed before the rehearsal touched anything. The earlier report of this is not answered by the new code: the new branch reports it as `unavailable` instead of `False`, but it still blames the run, still trips the whole-run retry, and on a repo with a slow writer it reproduces exactly the flake this change is meant to remove. The check should either ignore shards that were already unstable in `before`, or require the shard to have been readable/stable at the pre-run read before counting it as having moved.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py `judge_live` (`moved = live_moved(before, after)`)

chunk_findings.detail: Still holds; the diff does not answer prior finding 6. `write_diagnostics` stamps the file (name and `"run"` field) with `runs[-1].run_id` and serializes only the *final* report's `table`/`checks`, but flattens `"commands": [c for r in runs for c in r.commands]` across every run with no run attribution. Concretely: run1 detects a live change (and may carry a `FAIL`), the retry run2 also detects a change, so `write_diagnostics` is called; the emitted JSON is named/labelled with run2's id, yet its `commands` interleave run1's and run2's output and run1's step table and checks are silently gone. An operator reading the artifact to diagnose `B-dryrun-flake` cannot tell which run produced a given command or reconstruct the failing first run, even though `runs` was passed in precisely to carry that data.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py:write_diagnostics (called from run_all)

chunk_findings.detail: The retry discards the first run's evidence whenever the second run comes back clean. Given a live writer that rewrites a shard during the first rehearsal (so `report.facts["live_changed"]` is set, `first` is captured, and the whole run is retried), and that stops before the retry, run2 produces a clean report; the condition `if any(c.status == FAIL for c in report.checks) or report.facts.get("live_changed")` is then false on the *final* report, so `write_diagnostics` is never called. The two `Rehearsal` objects in `runs` (including run1's commands, the only capture of the flake) are dropped, and the docstring of the same function — "A failed run (or a project that moved) leaves its step table and every command's output in a file" — is violated: a project did move (run1 recorded it, and only the summary string `first_run` survives). The condition needs to also fire when the run was retried (e.g. `"first_run" in report.facts`), otherwise the one scenario this change exists to diagnose produces no artifact at all.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py:run_all (diagnostics condition)

In the motivating case — run1 sets `live_changed`, the whole run is retried, run2 also sees a change — the emitted file is stamped with run2's id but contains run1's commands, and run1's step table and checks are dropped, so the diagnostic the operator is sent to cannot explain the first failure. chunk_findings.detail:
For a retried rehearsal — precisely the case
`test_a_rewritten_live_shard_is_a_named_unavailable_result_after_one_retry` sets up (run 1 detects a moved live shard, run 2 detects it again, final unavailable) — `write_diagnostics` stamps the file and its `"run"` field with `runs[-1].run_id`, serializes only the last report's `table`/`checks`, and flattens `commands` from every run with no run attribution. Run 1's step table, its checks, and the association of its commands to run 1 are therefore absent from the artifact that the failure line tells the operator to open, so the diagnostician cannot tell which attempt produced which output. The new test only asserts the final row and `exit_code == 2`; it never opens the persisted JSON, so it does not answer this.

chunk_findings.detail: `MAX_COMMANDS = 300` bounds the transcript to the last commands, but the failure report added to `Result.render` prints `diagnostics (every step's stdout and stderr): <path>` and the module bullet promises "every command's bounded stdout and stderr". Given a real upgrade dry run that emits more than 300 commands, the earliest commands' output — possibly the failing step's — is silently missing from the file, so the pointer the operator is given overstates what is there. `test_a_failed_dry_run_persists_its_table_and_each_steps_stderr` uses a 10-step run and only checks that the second command's output is present, so it never exercises the cap.

chunk_findings.detail: The two comments state opposite precedence: `DIAG_ENV`'s comment says "this variable, else `--diag-dir`, else `.ddflow/local/dryrun/`" (env beats the explicit flag), while the `Options.diag_dir` field comment says a set field wins and the env var is only the fallback. An operator who passes `--diag-dir` while `DDFLOW_DRYRUN_DIAG_DIR` is exported in their shell will look in one directory and the artifact will be in the other. `test_the_diagnostics_go_to_the_local_directory_unless_told_otherwise` only sets the env var (never `diag_dir`), so the two paths are never both populated and the conflict is not disambiguated.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/upgrade_dryrun.py:DIAG_ENV vs Options.diag_dir
